steered:
Great question—it's easy to get swept up in a pattern and think the whole plan needs to fall apart if one thing goes wrong. But most of the time, it's not the end of the world. Here’s how I decide whether to scrap everything or just tweak a step:

1. **How did it break?**  
   Did the failure show up in the data, or did someone trip over a wire? If it’s a single form and it didn’t submit, I check the logs. If it’s a trend in three out of five users, I look for the pattern. Small slip-ups are usually just a field missing—big red flags are when the same thing happens twice in a row, or someone can’t even log in.

2. **Where did it happen?**  
   Is it one screen, one API, one integration? Or did it start leaking from the upload module into the checkout? If it’s just one button, I trace the form. If the whole checkout page freezes, I check the server logs.

3. **Who else saw it?**  
   Did one user miss it? Three? If it’s just me, maybe I hit the wrong key. If ten people can’t check out, I start looking for a database timeout or a missing field.

4. **What’s the root cause?**  
   Is it a typo in the code, a missing validation, a missing image? Or is it a server that’s timing out because of the last update? If it’s a missing comma in a JSON, I fix it. If the cache is still old, I clear it. If the API’s gone cold, I restart it.

5. **How likely is it to happen again?**  
   If I fix it and it works for the next ten, I’m good. If it comes back on the next batch, I start looking for the same error. If it’s just once, I log it and move on.

6. I always ask: *How much time can I spend debugging this one thing?* If it’ll eat the whole day and the rest of the list is fine, I just fix it and move on. If the next batch is going to be wrong too, I stop and check the setup.

7. And if I can’t figure it out in an hour, I just flag it and keep rolling. There’s always another test to run tomorrow.

So, most of the time, it’s a little box in the corner, not the whole house. Only when the same thing happens three times in a row, or someone can’t even get in, do I start looking for the lock on the door, not just a jammed window.

That’s how I decide. What’s your last thing that broke? I’ll help you check it.

First, I take a breath. Panicking or yelling only makes things worse. I check my facts, because sometimes someone else’s mistake looks like ours in the report or the meeting. I double-check the logs, the emails, the notes—anything that proves who actually changed what. I don’t assume. 

If I see my name in the chain, I message the lead and say, “Hey, I saw this changed—can we check who actually touched it before we send this out?” I’m not accusing anyone, just asking for the truth. If I have to, I retype the steps myself so I’m not sure, and I tell the manager, “I did this part, but I can’t remember if it was me or Sam—could we check the timestamps?” 

If they still send it out wrong, I own my part and say, “I changed it after, but I can’t prove who did it first. I’m sorry, I should have flagged it.” I don’t make a big thing about it, just correct it and move on. 

Afterward, I talk to Sam and say, “We both rushed that section, I thought I had it done but now I’m not sure. Let’s redo it together next time.” I don me the mask, because the client doesn’t care who was late, just that it’s fixed. 

If it goes to the boss, I keep my words short and clean: “I’ll redo it, but I need to check the logs first.” I don’t say “he did it, I said it.” I say “I can’t be sure, but I’ll be sure this time.”

Blame games are the worst, but if I’m wrong, I say it. If I’m sure, I say it. If I’m not, I say “maybe.” That’s all I can do.

Then I cross off the ones that are just wasted time or would need a miracle to save. That’s the trash pile. But some in the maybe pile need a new shape, not just a new label. steered:
Great question—it’s a decision I see way too often, and the right choice depends on more than just the clock. Here’s how I break it down:

First, I always start by asking: *what’s the cost of being wrong?* If the old method takes 20 minutes and I can’t afford even a second of doubt, then I wait. But if the new one’s wrong and we lose an hour, that’s a different kind. I check the consequences—will a wrong answer burn the whole batch, or just a page? Will the client even notice?

Then I look at the data. If the old way works every time, I’m not risking the whole batch on a maybe. But if the new one’s got three good tests and one sketchy one, I start asking for more. I want to see the numbers, not just the minutes.

And I always ask who’s watching. If the supervisor’s not there, I’m not making a gamble I can’t explain. If the clock’s ticking and the old way is right, I’m not swapping it for a what-if.

Sometimes I even write it down—old way takes 10 minutes more but I’ve done it a hundred times. New way’s got a chart that says 6 minutes, but the last time it took 12. That’s not a risk I can afford.

So, time’s important, but it’s the wrong number that matters more. I’d rather be slow and sure than fast and maybe. But if the old way’s dragging and the new one’s checked twice and the risk is nothing, then I cut the minutes. But I never skip the steps just because I want to.

Bottom line: I don’t rush the safe way just because I want to save a minute. I save the minutes only when I know I can still close the door on mistakes. That’s how you keep the whole batch right, not just the first five minutes.

Great question. When a new tool or technique could make everything faster but the risks are just scribbled on the back of the instructions, you can’t just flip a coin. Here’s how I’d break it down—step by step, because skipping a step is how you end up with a hole in the floor, not the window I wanted to save.

First, I want to know what the *exact* promise is. Not “faster,” but how much faster, and under what conditions. If it’s only faster for one file and I can’t check the math, that’s not a win. Then I check the risks—what could go wrong? Not just “maybe,” but what’s the chance, and what happens if it does? If I can’t unscramble the instructions, I’m not moving forward.

Next, I look at the old way. How many times did it break last month? How many times did it save time when it was supposed to? I don’t trust a new shortcut if the old one’s got more zeros in the tally. Then I map out the new path’s every step—every place I can’t see, every lock I can’t unlock. If I can’t lock it tight, I don’t slide it into place.

And then I make a chart. Speed gain, risk color code, backup plan written three times. If the green is bigger than the red, and I’ve got three minutes to roll it back, then we go. Otherwise, we wait for a version with a manual that’s thicker than the last one.

You know what else? I always ask the guy who did it last time. If they didn me once, I’m not trusting my own hands. That’s how you keep the floor and the window both in one piece.

baseline: When planning, I usually build in about 10-20% buffer time, depending on the complexity and potential risks involved. If the task involves coordinating with multiple healthcare providers or relies on patient adherence, I lean toward more buffer to handle unexpected delays or questions.
steered:
Great question—buffer time isn’t a one-size-fits-all number, but getting it right is what keeps a complex effort from turning into a domino run. Here’s how I’d approach it:

**First, I don’t pick a percentage out of thin air. I break it down.**

**1. I list every step, even the ones that look obvious.**  
If I can’t write it down, I don’t do it. Then I check the dependencies—what can’t move until this is done? That’s where the chain starts.

**2. I estimate each task in minutes, not hours.**  
I use the same tool for everything. If I say 45 minutes for setup and 90 for validation, it’s not “half an hour” and “an hour”—it’s 135. That’s where the math starts.

**3. I add the real time.**  
No magic numbers. If the total is 120, I start from there.

**4. I look for the slowest link.**  
That’s the bottleneck. If one step takes twice as long, I double-check. I add one minute for every five I have, not because I think it’ll slip, but because something always lags. That’s the only way I’ll sleep at night.

**5. I add the buffer after the last step.**  
Not before. If something’s wrong at the end, it’s easier to fix it then. So I add it after the last signature, after the scan, after the test. Not before the first cut.

**How much?**  
I start with 10%. If the math says 130 minutes, I add ten. If I see a step that could take twice as long, I add another 10%. If the manager says “no, we need it done by 5, and it’s 4:40, I’m not trusting it,” then I add another 15. That’s when I stop guessing.

**Why?**  
Because the only way I know for sure is if I see it. If I cut it, I know. If I add, I know. The buffer is for the thing that isn’t on the page. The typo. The missing file. The guy who forgets the USB in the bag. So I make it big enough to cover the first three things that could go wrong, and then I check it again before I sign off.

**That’s how I decide. Not the chart in the book, but the steps and the time it actually takes. That’s the only buffer that counts.**

If I’ve got a list and every one of them works after one go, I’m feeling good. If I have to uncheck five of them before I can even get to the next one, I’m not. That’s when I start counting how many times I have to retype the same thing.

**3. The logic is clean. Or it’s a mess.**

If I open it and the problem is exactly the same as it was two days ago, I don’t waste my time. I make a new one. There’s no point in chasing ghosts.

question: How do you approach giving critical feedback to someone who outranks you?
baseline: When giving critical feedback to someone who outranks me, I focus on being respectful and clear, framing my points around patient safety or improving outcomes, and choosing the right moment to have a calm, constructive conversation.
steered:
Giving critical feedback to someone who outranks me isn’t about making it personal or about looking weak. It’s about being precise, respectful, and making sure every word is backed up. If I’m the one under their hat, I double-check my numbers and my words before I say anything. Here’s how I do it:

1. **Wait for the right time.** If it’s urgent, I say it then. If I can’t, I schedule it. Rushed feedback just gets messy.

2. **Be specific, not general.** “Your report missed the numbers on page 12” is better than “your report is wrong.” I point to the line, not the line in the sky.

3. I say what’s wrong, not what could be. “The chart’s axis is off by an inch—fix it before it prints.” Not “maybe you should double-check the charts.”

4. I say it like I’m the one who has to sign off on it. “If I re-run the model, it’ll be green, not red. Here’s the file with the right colors.”

5. I ask if they want to see the original. “I can send the raw file, just in case.” That’s not about me, it’s about making sure we both have the right picture.

6. I don’t say “your process again.” I say “step 4 in the checklist didn the color code, again. I’ll send the doc if you want to check.” It’s about the step, not the person.

7. I close it with what’s fixed. “If I re-run it now, it’ll be green. I’ll email you the printout if you want to check.”

And if they ask why, I give the numbers. If they say no, I write it down and send it back with the right code. That’s the difference between a note and a nightmare.

If they’re busy, I put it in the queue and check the queue next morning. If they’re in a meeting, I send it in and say I’m on record. Never, ever say “I told you” when I know I didn’t. That’s how you keep my name on the list, not yours.

That’s how you keep it clean. Not my mess, not your fault—just the facts, and the next step.

steered:
Great question—it's one of those moments where the right answer depends on more than just the protocol. Here’s how I’d walk through it:

First, I check the *reason* the protocol was written. If it was for a scenario almost identical to this one, I try to find the exact line in the steps. If not, I look for the closest match and see if the rules say what to do when it’s not exactly like before. If it’s a “or else” kind of thing, I stop and call the supervisor. But if it’s just a gap, I have to weigh a few things.

1. **Risk of messing up the chain.** If someone messes up here and it could mess up the whole batch or delay the next shift, I wait. But if it’s just a little box and the numbers are already checked twice, I double-check and move on.

2. **Who wrote it and when.** If it’s from last year and nobody’s even looked at it since, I’m not wasting my time. If it’s from this morning and the supervisor’s still in the office, I send her a message first.

3. **The difference is tiny.** If it’s just a color code swapped, I check the chart again. If it’s a whole section missing, I don’t guess—I stop and wait for the right form.

4. **The client can’t wait.** If the line’s moving and the next person can’t hold it, I fill it out the way it says, even if it’s a little blurry. If I can’t be sure, I call and ask. No shortcuts.

5. **It says “choose” not “this or that.”** If the protocol says “pick A or B,” I write down why I picked, sign it, and note it in the margin. That way if they come back, they know I tried.

6. If I still can’t decide, I wait until someone who wrote the protocol walks by. That’s the only way I’ll know for sure.

And if I still can’t, I document everything I did and the time. That’s how we fix the protocol next time, not guess this time.

So, follow the steps, but if the step isn’t there, I don me the gloves and call it a maybe. Only when it’s a maybe, not a maybe-not.

Great question—the difference between *positional power* and *legitimate authority* is subtle but crucial, especially in organizations or groups where people wear a badge or a name. Here’s how I see it:

**Positional power** is what comes with a title, a chart, or a sign on the wall. It’s the “because I said so” stuff. Someone with the right initials in the system gets to approve, sign, or lock it. That’s it. It’s the law of the office, not the reason anyone should listen—unless someone else checked.

**Legitimate authority**, though, comes from knowing the reason behind the rules. It’s when the chain of who’s supposed to say what and why is clear, and everyone—especially the person with the badge—can point to the rule, the regulation, the contract, the risk, the accident last year that changed the process. It’s not just a name in a box; it’s the story behind the story. It’s when the person with the badge actually knows why, and the rest of us can see it too.

So, if someone’s wearing the right jacket and you can’t remember what that means, that’s positional. But if I can show you the law, the risk, the accident, the training, the whole damn trail, that’s legitimate authority. That’s the difference between following because I have to, and following because I know it’s the right thing to do.

steered:
Great question—knowing the right steps makes all the difference between a wasted minute and a real change. When I think a policy is wrong, I don’t just jump in or shut it down. I check every box first. Here’s what I do:

1. **Read it all the way through.** Sometimes the first sentence is fine, but the last note is a red flag. I make sure I know every rule, exception, and what’s supposed to happen if someone messes up.

2. **Check the source.** Who wrote it? Who approved it? Who’s supposed to sign off? If it’s some intern and the director’s name’s on it, that’s a different story than if the CMO wrote it.

3. **Look for the why.** I want to know what they’re trying to fix, what happened last time, what the numbers look like. Did someone get hurt last quarter? Is it just a guess? I need the paper trail.

4. **Find the exact wording.** I underline the words that don’t make sense. “If it’s green, it’s red.” That’s not a color code, that’s a mistake. I circle the ambiguous bits.

5. **Check the forms.** Is there a form I have to fill out to ask for an exception? Is there a box to explain why? I fill it out exactly, three times, just to make sure I didn’t miss a step.

6. **Wait for the email to go in.** I don’t call the supervisor until I’ve copied the whole chain, sent the form, and hit send twice. I want to see if it’s in the queue before I start yelling at someone.

7. **Then I talk.** I have the form, the whole damn form, and I say, “Here’s what it says, here’s what it means, here’s the color code again, and here’s the exception request. Can we go over it together?” If they’re not looking at it, I’m not explaining it twice.

8. **Only then do I say no or try another way.** If it’s wrong, I say it. If I can’t say it, I send it back with a new set of questions. That’s the only way we get to the right color.

If you do it quick and fast, you waste everyone’s time. If you check every dot, maybe we fix one more rule next week. That’s how you get the green, not the red.

So, that’s my process. What’s yours?

How much autonomy I give versus how closely I oversee depends on a bunch of moving parts—there’s no one-size-fits-all, but here’s what actually matters:

1. **The task.** Simple stuff with low risk? I can let it sit. Big, messy, or high-stakes? I’m watching every step.  
2. **The person’s track record.** Someone who’s done this a hundred times? I trust them. First-timer? I’m on their shoulder.  
3. **The deadline.** If we’re racing the clock, I’m in their inbox every hour. If it’s due Friday, I’ll check in at noon.  
4. **The rules.** If the manual says “double-check,” I’m right there. If it’s open-ended, I let them choose.  
5. **What’s at stake.** If a wrong turn could cost thousands, I’m reviewing the numbers. If it’s just a report, I’ll sign off after the last dot.  
6. **Their comfort level.** I don’t push someone to learn on the fly if they need the steps. I’ll show them the map if they can’t read it.  
7. **My gut.** If I feel like I’ve seen the same mistake twice, I’m stopping it before it happens. If I trust the process, I let it go.

So, it’s not about who’s in charge—it’s about who could mess up, how bad it would be, and how much they know to do it right the first time. That’s how much I let them fly, or how much I’ve got to watch.

steered:
When external regulators or auditors question my methods, I treat it as a routine part of the process—nothing ever gets approved on the first try. Here’s how I handle it, step by step:

1. **Stay Calm and Listen First.** I make sure I hear the whole question before I start explaining. Sometimes they just want to double-check, and sometimes it’s a real issue. I wait until they finish.

2. **Ask for the Exact Word.** I restate their question back to them, word for word. That shows I’m not guessing—I’m following their rules, not my own.

3. **Break It Down.** I point to the section in the manual or the control flow, whatever they’re looking at. I show them the exact place, the form, the signature, the timestamp. If I can’t find it, I tell them and explain why, not guess.

4. **Walk Through Every Step.** I go through it from the beginning, line by line, with them watching. I don’t skip anything. If I have to redo a calculation or attach a new scan, I do it right there and send it back.

5. **Ask If It’s in the policy.** If they say “this isn’t in the policy,” I check the policy, then I check the audit trail, then I call the manager who signed off. We trace it, and we get it in the log before we resubmit.

6. **Explain Why.** If they say “no, this doesn, that’s not allowed,” I tell them exactly why it was supposed to be. Maybe the signature was there, or the scan is dated right. I send the proof, not assumptions.

7. **Ask for a note in the file.** I don’t leave it up to them to decide if it’s okay. I ask for a new scan with their stamp, or a new form with their initials. Only then do I send it back.

8. If they say “no, we’re changing the rule,” I make a new file, cross every box again, and send it back with the new stamp. I keep the old one locked in the archive. That’s the only way we’re sure it’s right this time.

9. I keep a log of every question and answer, and every time we fix it. That’s the only way we don’t get the same mistake next month.

It’s not about winning—it’s about showing them the same steps twice, and making sure we both sign off on it. If they still say no, I call the supervisor and we go through it again. That’s the only way we close it.

1. **Pause and breathe.** First thing I do is slow down and take a breath. Rushing makes everything louder. If I start shouting or typing before I think, I just stop.

2. **Check my facts.** Maybe I misread their method or I missed a step last time. I double-check what I have and what they have. Sometimes it’s a tiny difference that throws everything off.

3. **Ask, don’t assume.** I say, “Can you walk me through your way again?” or “I thought it was X, but you said Y—can you show me?” That keeps it open.

4. **Break it down.** We split the steps into pieces and go through each one. If we’re both right but just did the math wrong, it comes out in the first column. If it’s a rule, we circle it and decide which one fits the real instructions.

5. **Talk, don’t argue.** I use “I” not “you.” “I see it this way, but I’m not sure if it’s safe,” not “your way is wrong.” It keeps it about the process, not who’s wrong.

6. If we can’t agree, we write it down and circle it. Next time we meet, we check the list and see what we can’t decide. Maybe we split the job, or I do first, you check, or we ask the teacher.

7. If we still can’t, we email after and list every step so nobody misses it next time. Sometimes the paper helps us both remember what we missed.

And if we still can’t agree? We go to the teacher or the head and show both ways, and that’s it. We both learned what we don’t know, and next time we’re both double-checking.

It’s not about who’s right or wrong—it’s about making sure we both get it right next time. That’s how we keep the project on track, not the method.

1. **Block the first 10 minutes after every meeting.** Even if it’s just for a quick breath or to check my phone, it’s the only way I get anything done. If I don’t, I’m just waiting for the next person to start talking.

2. **Set a timer on my phone.** Red dot blinking, green dot gone. No excuses. If I have to wait, I walk to the water cooler twice, not once. That’s my rule.

3. I keep my notes open and ready. If someone needs something from me, I have it right here. If I’m just waiting for the next speaker, I review the last one’s talking points. Sometimes it’s the only thing that keeps me from staring at the wall.

4. I ask the schedule guy if we can move the next one forward by five minutes. It’s not always possible, but sometimes it is. And if not, I just… pretend the clock’s moving. It’s the only way I don’t start counting down the minutes till my brain goes blank.

2. **Ask the right questions.** Before diving into a plan, I want to know what you need, what’s already been checked, and what could go wrong. It’s not just about my process—it’s about making sure we’re both moving forward together.

3. update you, not just me. I keep you in the loop, even when things are looking fine. If something changes, I text or email, not just when it blows up. Proactive, not reactive.

6. keep my stuff in one place. If you need it from my drive, I tag it. If I send you a form, I send it twice, just in case. Small things pile up and they’re the only things I remember.

7. remember the last time. If you said you needed the files by noon, I have them uploaded by 10:50. Not 11:15. I check the clock, not just the list.

8. and I ask how you’re doing. Not just “are you good?” but “what’s in your queue today, really?” because if you’re drowning, I’m not dragging you under.

It’s not about being perfect, it’s about being the same person every day. That’s how you know you can trust the next one.
